It is the proof the debt is being paid.” — The core doctrine of the Church of the Five Sufferings OpenWorld's story takes place in a world that believes in the Church of the Five Sufferings . Several hundred years ago the sun vanished for a time, an event known as the Long Night . The saint Astra bore five holy torments, and the sun rose again. As the game begins, the days are once more growing shorter by the day. The player comes down from the mountain with the fairy Lumi at their side, is named a pilgrim by the Church, and sets out to find the five Seal-bearers . The authority for the lore is the collaborator's document The Church of the Five Sufferings: Setting and Main Story ; the full text is at Original Lore Document . This site only splits that text into pages, arranges them and links them to one another; it does not write new lore. Anything not yet settled in the original or in the team's discussions is marked “To be designed”. The official history This is the account every piece of evidence supports early in the game, and the account the game's characters believe (the original, §8, calls it “the first layer of understanding”): Long ago the days grew shorter and shorter until the sun vanished altogether. Crops withered, beasts turned strange, and the dead found no rest. This calamity is called the Long Night ; the people in the game call it “the First Long Night”. s: The main story's three layers of understanding, its chapter structure, and the parts built so far.
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. OpenWorld's main story is a pilgrimage: the protagonist is named a pilgrim by the Church of the Five Sufferings and sets out to find the five Seal-bearers , recover the five Instruments of the Sufferings , and finally hold the Great Rite of the Five Sufferings again in the Holy City . The story is understood in three layers: the early game is the official history, and after it come two reversals. Each chapter faces one Seal-bearer. The game currently goes as far as Chapter 1 (the First Seal: the Crown of Thorns). For how to play it step by step, see Main Quest Walkthrough . The first layer of understanding Astra is the saint who saved the world (§8). Early in the game, every piece of evidence supports the official history: Astra really did appear during the Long Night , really did bear the Five Sufferings , and when the fifth was complete the sun really did rise again. So players and ordinary townsfolk alike naturally believe that Astra saved the world. The player's mission is to repeat his miracle of long ago. When the game begins, several hundred years have passed since the first Long Night. The nights are lengthening again, and the Church has declared that the Seal-bearers can no longer hold. The protagonist is given a mission: to set out on the pilgrimage, find the five Seal-bearers, defeat them now that their Seals have twisted them, recover the five Instruments of the Sufferings, and finally travel to the Holy City and hold the Great Rite of the Five Sufferings again (§7). s: The religion Astra's followers founded: its doctrine, creed, relics and organization.
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. “Suffering is not God's abandonment. It is the proof the debt is being paid.” — The Church of the Five Sufferings The Church of the Five Sufferings is the religion founded by Astra 's followers, and the prevailing faith of this world. People saw with their own eyes Astra bear the Five Sufferings , and after the fifth they saw the sun again, so they came to believe that “Astra repaid the world's calamity with his own pain.” His five instruments of torment were enshrined as the highest relics (the Instruments of the Sufferings ), and so the Church of the Five Sufferings was founded. Doctrine The core doctrine (§1): Suffering is not God's abandonment. Suffering is the proof the debt is being paid. The creed (§5). Over time, the Church's most central creed became: “Suffering brings one nearer to God.” “As long as someone goes on bearing the Five Sufferings, the Long Night will never fall again.” The original lore text says the second line is “not entirely wrong.” The theology of creation (§2): God did not truly create light; he only separated light from the First Night . The sun is the boundary that keeps them apart. The meaning of the Five Sufferings : the Church has its own reading of each Suffering; the Crowning, for instance, is “giving up human pride and will”, and the Nailing is “accepting death”. See the Five Sufferings . In the game, the doctrine is spoken mostly by Sister Ilse . She recites it on the night of thanks and at ordinary times: Suffering is not God's abandonment. I

x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. The First Night (原夜) is, in the Church of the Five Sufferings setting, a darkness older than the world. The sun keeps light and the First Night apart; when the First Night seeps back into reality, the days grow shorter until at last the sun vanishes, and that is the Long Night . The Church's theology of creation The later theology of creation of the Church of the Five Sufferings holds: God did not truly “create” light. God only separated light from the First Night. On this account, the sun is not the First Night's opposite but a boundary that keeps the separation in place. That boundary is not stable forever. The First Night seeps into reality Over long ages, the First Night seeps back into reality. The signs the original lore text lists are: dusk comes earlier; dawn comes later; the days grow gradually shorter; the noon sunlight grows paler and paler; plants and animals begin to behave strangely; the dead cannot fully rest; creatures that do not belong to the real world appear at night. If the erosion goes on, the sun at last vanishes altogether, and that is the Long Night . So the Long Night is not a disaster caused by some demon lord; it is closer to an unavoidable, cyclical breakdown of the world itself. In the game The game's text does not yet use the word “First Night” for this darkness. The Nightbearer is an identity the Church of the Five Sufferings setting reveals only late in the main story. It explains the true place of the Five Sufferings , the Seal-bearers and Astra in this world, and it decides the Ending . Almost everything on this page concerns the main story's second reversal. Readers who have not played that far and do not want to know can read the first layer of understanding in Main Story first. What the Nightbearer is (click to show) The Vessel During the first Long Night, Astra discovered that “the First Night cannot be destroyed,” but that it can be “given a vessel.” If a living being strong enough carries the whole of the First Night within itself, the First Night can no longer invade the world (§3). An ordinary person's body and soul cannot withstand such power, so Astra designed the Five Sufferings: each one remakes an ordinary person into a being able to hold the First Night: wearing down the boundaries of self, adapting the flesh to pain and transformation, cutting the dependence on food and sleep, fastening the person to reality, and at last opening an “entrance” at the heart (§3, §4). Astra was the first Nightbearer. He locked the First Night inside himself and for centuries, neither dead nor alive, has existed as a vast vessel (§10). The rule of the world “The First Night cannot be killed.” It can only be “carried”. The world must always have a Nightbearer (§11). x: The Long Night is the calamity in which the sun gradually vanishes and the world sinks into an endless dark. The first Long Night, several hundred years ago, was ended by Astra ; the people in the game call that one “ the First Long Night ”. As the game begins, the days are growing shorter again, and the Church has declared that the Long Night is coming back. The first Long Night (the First Long Night) Long ago the sun gradually vanished, and the days grew shorter and shorter until the whole world sank into an endless dark. Crops withered, beasts turned strange, the dead found no rest, and human civilization was all but destroyed. People tried nearly everything: war, magic, sacrifice and prayer, and none of it truly stopped it. At the worst of the Long Night, the saint Astra appeared and willingly bore five holy torments (the Five Sufferings ). When the fifth torment was complete, the sun rose again and the Long Night ended. In the game, Sister Ilse of Firstlight Village tells the story like this: Long ago the days grew shorter and shorter, until one morning the sun did not rise at all. The crops died. The beasts changed. The dead found no rest. That was the First Night. The morning the First Long Night ended has left several place names and relics in the game: Firstlight Village takes its name from the first dawn after the First Long Night. The village's fire (the First Fire) is said to have been taken from that day's first ray of dawn. The dawnstone on Dawn Hill is carved “HERE THE SUN ROSE AGAIN”. Chapter 3 , by the structure of the main story, is the chapter of the Third Seal: the protagonist faces the third Seal-bearer , Ehle, Priest of the Black Scale , and recovers the third Instrument of the Sufferings , the Scales of Hunger. The chapter's places, people, quests and boss fight have not yet been designed, and it is not in the game yet. What is already decided Seal-bearer : Ehle, Priest of the Black Scale, holder of the Third Seal, modeled on the rider on the black horse among the first five seals of the Book of Revelation (§6). Torment : the Third Suffering, the Starving . Astra gave up food and drink and let his body be weighed on the scales against grain, against sin and against life. Scripture preserves one line: “His flesh at last weighed less than sin.” The Church reads it as “freedom from the desires of the flesh” (§4). Instrument of the Sufferings : the Scales of Hunger . Chapter structure : one Seal-bearer per chapter; when the Seal-bearer falls, Lumi catches part of the Seal's power and gains a Boon ; and the nights grow a little longer again. It is the proof the debt is being paid.” — Astra's altar, Firstlight Village Astra is the saint who appeared at the worst of the first Long Night . He willingly bore five holy torments (the Five Sufferings ), and when the fifth was complete, the sun rose again. Later ages honored him as Astra, the First Martyr . His followers founded the Church of the Five Sufferings , and the five instruments of torment used on him became its highest relics (the Instruments of the Sufferings ). In the main story's design, he is also the final boss. The official history When the first Long Night fell, people tried war, magic, sacrifice and prayer, and none of it truly stopped it. Astra appeared and bore, one after another, the Crowning, the Scourging, the Starving, the Nailing and the Piercing. At the moment the holy lance pierced his chest, the sun rose again, and the Long Night ended. People believed that “Astra repaid the world's calamity with his own pain.” Later, the Church divided the power of the five holy instruments among five Seal-bearers , who share Astra's pain. Early in the game, every piece of evidence supports this account. Players and ordinary townsfolk alike naturally believe that Astra saved the world, and the player's mission is to repeat his miracle of long ago (§8). s: How the main line goes from start to finish: seven main quests one after another — Waking in the tut
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. This page sets out, in order, how to play through the main line. The main line is a chain of main quests : when one ends the next begins by itself, with no one to talk to, and there is always one under way. A new game wakes on Cloudtop and goes down from the mountain to The Ford and Firstlight Village ; Chapter 1's Lost in the Barrow , The Vigil and The First Seal lead up to the defeat of The White Knight Alberic , and The Crown of Thorns brings the Crown of Thorns back to the village; after that comes the old main line from before Chapter 1, The Dragon Road , through Emberfall to the dragon of Cinder Peak . The main quest under way is the tracked quest by default: the tracker in the top-right corner of the screen lists its unfinished objectives, markers on the minimap, the world map and the edges of the screen point to where to go, and the quest journal ( L ) records every step you have taken. Press E on Lumi and she tells you the current objective and a hint. Each step's objective is a state, not a fixed route: whatever way you reach it counts. Besides the main line, Lumi begins a few guide quests when the moment is right (skill points, professions, fishing, farming); they are listed alongside the main line in her panel and do not affect the main line's tracking. Story content is kept inside spoiler blocks. For the story itself see Main Story and Chapter 1 . s: OpenWorld's design principles: the world is code, goals are states, places teach, systems are genera
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. This page records the principles OpenWorld's design follows. Each one notes the decision it comes from. For how a particular system works, see that system's page. The world is code, and it learns what it has never seen The game's state and rules are code, and the game is a complete, ordinary game in itself: it can be played from start to finish without AI. When you do something no rule defines, the world asks an AI, writes the answer down as a rule and keeps it, and from then on every player's world responds that way. See The World Learns . There is only one AI interface: the outcome of an event. If it is defined, the rule applies; if not, the AI is asked; with no AI, an error or a time-out, the default outcome of that place applies (usually nothing happens). A rule writes only itself. A rule belongs to one class of things (its “host”); it can read anything but change only itself. To affect something else, it sends that thing an event, and the thing answers by itself. Lava's rule is “send scorching to whatever is on top”; a person's rule is “lose health when scorched”; what a fire slime does when scorched is up to its own rule, and if that is undefined, the AI is asked. Patches only fill gaps; they never change behavior that is already defined. A learned rule belongs to one kind of thing only and fills only the place it was asked about; what holds for a whole class of things is written into the game's own rules. The same question is asked only once. Taking and putting are physics

x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. The Wild is the land cells of the Lands of the Five Seals that hold no story location. Each is a 40×30 map, shaped by that cell's ground and the world seed. In a given world, the same cell is the same map every time you go in; only the places the player has changed inside it are remembered. Frostfang Coast has five kinds of wild, one for each of its five walkable grounds; the other regions' grounds each have their own wilds, and the same ground may also differ from region to region (see Wilds of the Other Regions below). On the world map, the location markers bear names like “The wild plains” and “The wild forest”; once you walk in, the map itself is called “Open Plains”, “Deep Woods” and so on. Map Wild maps have no fixed layout, so there is no map template. Every one is 40×30, open on all four sides with no exit tiles: walk off any edge and you are back on that cell of the world map. Within a radius of 3 tiles of the map's center no trees grow and no rocks are placed, so there is always open ground under your feet when you walk in from the world map. The Wild is an open-air combat zone . After nightfall night creatures appear (at most 4 ). x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. “Did you see that? It answered!” — Lumi The world learns is the heart of OpenWorld. Everything in this world is decided by written rules: an axe chops a tree, fire lights dry grass, rain puts out what is burning, a person takes the bread you hand them. But no one can write everything in advance. When the player does something whose outcome no rule has defined, and the game is connected to an AI, the world pauses for a moment while the AI writes a new rule for what happens when this kind of thing meets this event; once it checks out, it is woven into the world. From then on the same kind of thing meeting the same event has a definite outcome, and no one who does it again needs to ask the AI. Every rule the world learns is recorded in the Threadbook , shared by every save and every player. Without an AI, the game is still a complete game that can be played from start to finish. Anything undefined is handled by default, which usually means nothing happens. What “something it has never seen” means Everything in the world carries its own rules, which say how it responds when others do something to it. For example: a tree states what happens when an axe chops it: it loses durability, and when felled becomes a stump and logs; dry grass states that it catches fire when fire touches it; a person states that they talk when someone presses E on them, and accept something handed to them with G . x: Villagers have satiety just as you do, only it drops half as fast. Two meals a day Everyone eats twice a day: in the hour after they get up and in the hour before bed. Those who live in a home of their own eat beside their household's larder; those with no home (who sleep at the shelter or out of doors) eat wherever mealtime finds them, carrying on with what they were doing ( Hesper eats by her fire). At mealtime, anyone not full (satiety under ninety percent) eats what they carry, or takes food from their own or their household's chests and barrels. They never take from another household's, and never buy or steal for a meal. The larder : every household with a house keeps a barrel or chest of bread and apples, by head: two loaves and an apple per person per day. Every morning it is topped back up, from what the household's work brings in. Take from it, and that household goes a meal short that day. While you are away : when you go to another map, the people there keep their days and their meals. When you come back, their satiety runs from their last meal, so they are not half-starved on your return. In the backdrop's towns, people eat one meal at noon at their own table, and their rooms' larders are topped up each day too. Hungry When a villager's satiety falls below sixty percent they are “hungry,” and they put down what they are doing to look for food, in this order: If they carry food , they eat it. x: As in The Elder Scrolls , the people of OpenWorld are of two kinds: Those the story cannot do without (people named in quests, cutscenes and story rules, and the profession trainer Bram ) don't die when their health drops to zero; they only fall down for half an hour and then wake with half their health. Someone who is down is not attacked again. People a quest names to protect : while a quest is under way, the people it names have the same protection, until the quest ends. For example, the person who gives a side quest and the person you are sent to find, or the guard entrusted to you in The Night-born . Everyone else can die. At present that is Cass , Tam and Vigo . Ordinary villagers added later can die by default too. When the player's health reaches zero you fall down and the death screen appears; see Health and Difficulty . After death When someone dies: Whoever struck them down gains experience (as much as their maximum health). They become a body lying where they fell. Everything they carried or held in their hands is inside the body. The body belongs to their household (to themselves, if they had no home): taking things from it is taking what belongs to others, and if seen it counts as theft . Two days later the body turns to bones , with the things still inside. Their schedule, their lines and their following all end with them. They never come back. s: People and monsters keep away from what harms them: one on fire runs to wet ground, one standing whe
x: The people and monsters of the world know what is bad for them and find a way to keep away from it or put it right. This is not a reaction written for rain and another for fire: a person reads the world's own rules — what happens if they stand here, touch this, use that — so rules the world learns later count just the same (see The World Learns ). What counts as bad What harms : bearing it costs health now and then, for example burning . This is a danger and comes before everything else (except a boss in a boss fight): it is seen to before schedules, fights and anything else. What is only unpleasant : wet , oiled , frozen , hungry . People deal with it before going to work, but never at the cost of something that harms. Health under half : they look for something or somewhere that heals. The place underfoot : if standing there makes them worse (standing on a burning cell, out in the rain), the trouble is the place, and leaving puts it right. Not everyone minds the same things: farmers, guards, fishers, hunters, soldiers, sailors and ferrykeepers work out in the wind and rain and do not mind getting wet. What they do They take the easiest of these: Leave : get away from the place that makes them worse, for example step off a burning cell, or go somewhere covered when it rains. If there is nowhere near, they go back to one of their own places (home, the house they work in), as long as it does not have the same trouble. Translate it . 每样物品都有一个 标准价 ，全世界只有这一套。商人的开价和收价、 Trading stall 和杂货铺的标价、 送礼 的心意、 罚金 ，都从这个数出发（见 Trading ）。 两条规矩 不用做的东西，按世界给出它的辛苦定价。 采来的、种出来的、钓上来的、挖出来的、怪物掉的，还有只能找到的宝物，各有一个价，以“一天能挣多少钱”为准：村民身上一天几十枚 Dawnmark 。 东西 标准价 Stick 、 Stone 、 Cut Grass 、 Wildflower 0.5 Log 、 Coal 、 Wheat 2 Herb 6 Iron Ore 8 Leather Hide 12 Raw Fish 12 Bucket of Milk 20 Gold Ore 40 Gem 50 做出来的东西，值它用掉的原料，再加两成五的手工钱。 原料按它最初从世界来的价算：一块 Plank 算半根原木，不按木板自己的价算。所以一个 Bucket 值三块木板的原木和一把草，再加两成五，手工钱只算一次。加工链再长，也只算一次。 用配方做的，按配方算：一把 Club 是一根原木，一张弓是两根树枝和三把草，一把铁剑是两块 Iron Ingot 和一块木板。 烤、熔炼、装满、做奶酪这些把一样东西变成另一样的，也照样算：烤鱼值生鱼，铁锭值它的矿石，奶酪值牛奶。 一样东西有几种做法（铁剑和钢剑，蜂蜜或花瓣做的治疗药水），按最省的那种定价，所以哪种做法都不会比用掉的原料更值钱。 铁、钢、金、木头做的东西，按 Substances 乘上系数（铁 1、钢 1.9、金 5、木头 0.6）。金子的系数是 5，所以一块金矿石正好是铁矿石的五倍。 为什么刷不了钱 商人卖东西是标准价加两成五，收东西是标准价的一半；满心好感时，卖便宜三成，收多给两成（见 Trading ）。 所以就算买卖双方都是满心好感，买原料要花它价钱的 0.875 倍，做成东西再卖，最多只拿回原料价钱的 0.8625 倍。这已经算上了手工钱和最好的品质加成。一条加工链再长，手工钱也只算一次。也就是说， 买原料做东西再卖，永远拿不回本钱 。 自己采、自己挖、自己种的原料做成东西再卖，才有赚头：原料直接卖拿到它价钱的一半到六成，做成东西再卖能拿到七成五。 技能多给的产量（ 高效冶炼 多出的锭、奶酪师多出的奶酪），是那项技能自己的奖励，不受这条限制。 制作者的等级与手艺 找到的装备， Quality 和 等级 越高越值钱。自己做的不一样：做出来的东西只值它这一种、这种材料、普通品质、1 级时的标准价，再按品质加一点。 品质 加成 粗制 ×0.8 普通 ×1 精良 ×1.08 大师 ×1.15 遗誓、圣痕 ×1.15 所以一个 20 级的大师锻造一把剑，剑的攻击力照样是 20 级大师的，但只能卖剑本身的价钱。 不值一枚铜币的东西 商人不收连一枚铜币都不值的东西（树枝、石头、草、野花这一类），会说「这东西一个铜板都不值。」 全部物品的标准价 Item Group Standard price Priced from Merchants ask Merchants pay Crown of Thorns Relics 400 Given by the world (gathered, grown, caught, mined, dropped, only found) 500 200 The Oath-Thorn Relics 400 Given by the world (gathered, grown,

s: How quests begin, how you accept or decline them, how they move forward stage by stage, and how you
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. A quest is something the world wants you to do. Main quests begin by themselves as the story goes; side quests and commissions need someone to entrust them to you: a person with a yellow “!” over their head has something to ask of you. Press E on them, they explain what they want, and below the dialogue box “Accept: quest name” and “Not now (quest name)” are listed; only choosing to accept takes it on. Every quest is divided into several stages : when things in the world change, the quest moves forward a step and writes a line in its journal . Press L to open the quest journal; the tracker in the top right of the screen, the minimap, the world map and the markers at the screen's edge point to where the quest you are tracking wants you to go. Four kinds of quest Kind Where it comes from How it begins Examples Main The story itself By itself, without talking to anyone: when one main quest ends, the next takes over Down from the Mountain , The First Seal Side Someone's own business Talk to them and accept in the dialogue box Mia's Ring , The Old Templar Commission Something happening in the village right now, or a job there is every day Talk to the person asking and accept, or take it at the commission board A Bite to Eat , Wood for the Fire Guide Lumi teaching you a way to play She speaks up herself: it begins when the moment comes A Road of Your Own , The First Cast In the quest journal, every quest name has a small tag in front saying which kind it is. s: Everyone has an opinion of everyone else (−100 to 100), decided by what you have done to them and to
x: Everyone has an opinion of everyone else, from −100 (bitter hatred) to 100 (as close as family). Their opinion of you is your regard with them. You can tell it from what they do: whether they will follow you, whether they sell to you dear, whether persuading them or apologizing works, whether they avoid you when they see you. When you talk to them, beside the name in the dialogue box there is a word and a row of ten hearts : one heart for every 10 points of regard, rounded; a heart more than half full (5 points or more) is drawn whole and one less than half is drawn as half, so 95 points is ten full hearts. Hover over the hearts to see the exact number. Opinion Label −60 and below hostile −59 to −20 cold −19 to 19 neutral 20 to 49 friendly 50 and above close Opinions belong to each pair of people separately : Marta's opinion of you, her opinion of Vigo , and Vigo's opinion of Marta are each their own. The same goes between villagers. Where it starts Strangers start at 0 (neutral). Family and friends (as written in their relationships) and members of the same household start at 30 (friendly). What raises it What you do Change Talk to them +2 the first time each day Give them something ( G , or “I have something for you.” in conversation) Thirty percent of the thing's value plus 2 (a loaf of bread is about +3) Give them their favorite gift +30, once per person per day (giving the same thing again that day counts as an ordinary gift) Return something you took from them +5 (+8 by choosing “Give back what I took.” in conversation) Bribe them (10 Dawnmark ) +12 Apologize successf

s: OpenWorld is a single-player game with no online or co-op mode; but the rules the world learns are s
x: OpenWorld is a single-player game , played alone in the browser, with no online, co-op or versus mode. Everyone's saves are kept only in their own browser. The one thing players share is what the world learns . All players connected to the same AI service share one rule library: when someone does something the world has never seen and the world learns its outcome, the other players' worlds learn it too within about 15 seconds, and the next time the same kind of thing meets the same event, no one has to wait for the AI. So every player is helping everyone teach this world to be more complete. See The World Learns , Threadbook . History 2026-10-01: The AI service gained a shared rule library, and every game connected to it syncs regularly. 2026-10-09: A learned rule belongs to only one kind of thing (see The World Learns ). s: The six grades of quality for weapons, tools and gear (Crude, Normal, Fine, Masterwork, Vowbound, St
x: Quality is the grade of how well a weapon, tool or piece of gear is made, in six grades (a different thing from gear level : level 1–20 is how strong it is, quality how well made). The higher the quality, the higher its attack and defense, and the more affixes gear rolls. Quality is written before the name (such as “Fine Stone Axe”; Normal quality isn't written), and the color of the name in the tooltip also shows the quality. The first four grades can be crafted ; the top two can only be found. The six grades Quality Attack/defence × How obtained Crude ×0.8 Crafter's level below the recipe's Common ×1 Crafter's level at the recipe's Fine ×1.25 Crafter's level 3 or more above the recipe's Masterwork ×1.5 Crafter's level 6 or more above the recipe's Vowbound ×1.75 Only found, never made Stigmatic ×2 Only the Seal-bearers have them; never made Quality Name color in the tooltip How to get it Crude Grey The crafter's level is below the recipe's requirement Normal White The crafter's level meets the recipe's requirement Fine Yellow The crafter's level is 3 or more above the recipe's requirement Masterwork Cyan The crafter's level is 6 or more above the recipe's requirement Vowbound Purple Found only: things left by those who swore a vow Stigmatic Orange-red Found only: things the Seal-bearers carry For each grade's multiplier see the quality table at the start of this section. A thing's attack and defense = the form's own stat × the substance 's multiplier × the quality's multiplier × the level 's multiplier, rounded, at least 1. The number of affixes gear rolls: Crude 2, Normal

s: You carry two numbers: Karma (−100 to 100) and Faith (−100 to 100). Doing wrong moves Karma toward e
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. You carry two numbers, both shown in the backpack's stats panel (below your character portrait): Karma and Faith . Both start at 0, and both lie between −100 and 100. Beside them is a third, Luck ; see below. Karma The stats panel shows only its size, not its sign: Karma of 5 reads “Good +5,” dropping to −5 reads “Evil +5,” and 0 is “Neutral.” Good is green, evil dark red. How it falls (doing wrong) : every evil deed you commit lowers your Karma, whether or not anyone sees : whether people see only decides whether you are held in grudge or wanted ; you yourself know what you did. It falls by a quarter of the deed's weight in people's eyes: Evil deed Weight Karma Murder 100 −25 Assault 35 −9 Arson 30 −8 Pickpocketing 25 −6 Theft 15 −4 Vandalism 10 −3 Lockpicking 8 −2 Hitting someone who struck you first is not assault (self-defense). Taking things that have no owner and fighting monsters are not evil deeds. How it rises (doing good) : Completing a quest that helps someone (commissions, errands, anything after which they think better of you): +3. Giving back what you took (“Give back what I took.” in conversation): +2. Having an apology accepted: +1. What it does : it decides how fast regard grows (see Friendship ). Everyone also has their own leaning, decided by how honest they are: most villagers are good, light-fingered people like Vigo lean evil, and a boastful peddler like Tobin is in the middle. s: How everyone looks is assembled from one look record: the figure on the map, the anime-style portrai
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. A look is how a person appears. Everyone in the game (villagers, passers-by, the player, and in future the people the modding AI brings into the world) has a look record : one body, one part per slot, and one color per color key. The 24×36 pixel figure on the map, the anime-style bust portrait beside the dialogue box, the pictures in the codex and on the wiki, and the appearance tags that rules can recognize are all drawn and derived from this one record. When someone dyes their hair, it changes on the map, in the portrait and in the tags at the same time; the three can never disagree. The look record Part Contents Body Woman, man, girl, boy. Decides the figure's build on the map and the portrait's bust. Adult men and women share the same head, so the parts worn on the head fit both bodies Parts One per slot: hair, face, beard, age, mark, glasses, hat, cloak, armour, outfit. Hat, beard, mark and glasses can be left empty; cloak and armour appear only when something is worn Colors Hair color, eye color, skin color, and the parts' own colors (an outfit's main color, its second color, its leather or metal color, a hat's color). Beard and eyebrows follow the hair color One color colors both pictures at once: the map figure takes light, middle, dark and deepest shades from it; the portrait spreads it into a whole ramp from line art to highlight. So silver hair on the map and silver hair in the portrait are the same silver. Three outputs The map figure : a 24×36 pixel, two-cell-tall FFB

s: The three save slots in the browser, when the game autosaves, saving by hand, exporting and importin
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. OpenWorld keeps its saves in the browser , in three save slots. The game saves automatically, and you can also save by hand in the Options . A save can be exported as a file on your computer and imported again in another browser or on another computer. The threads the world has learned belong to no single save: all saves share them. Save slots There are three save slots: Slot 1, Slot 2 and Slot 3. Each slot's card shows: location · day and time · level · current objective (the first unfinished objective of the quest you are tracking, or the quest's name when there is none), for example “Cloudtop · Day 1 13:00 · Lv 1 · The shrine stone at the mountain's foot”, with the date and time it was saved below. An empty slot reads “Empty”. On Hardcore difficulty, a save that has ended reads “Hardcore · ended · location · day N” and can no longer be loaded. See Difficulty . “Continue” on the title page loads the most recently saved slot (skipping any that have ended). Starting a new game means choosing a slot. When the slot already holds progress, the button reads “Overwrite & start”, and the game first asks “Slot N already has progress. Overwrite it?”. s: OpenWorld has no seasons, and no weeks, months or years; the date counts only days, and the long-ter
x: OpenWorld has no seasons , and no weeks, months or years either. The date counts only “day N”, each day 24 hours long; see In-game Time . Crops do not keep to seasons: as long as they are in the open and watered on time, they grow. See Farming and Crops . Each day's weather is decided at random (the first two days are fixed), and does not change with the seasons. The villagers' schedules change only with the hour, the weather and the story; there is no difference between days of the week. The one long-term change in the world is the night: as the Seal-bearers fall one by one, dark comes earlier and dawn comes later. See Day and Night . History 2026-10-01: The early version modeled on Stardew Valley had days of the week and seasons. 2026-10-02: The team decided not to copy Stardew Valley's gameplay systems; weeks and seasons were removed, leaving only the day count and day and night. 2026-10-06: Added nights that grow longer with the story. s: Every key and mouse action: four inputs (left click, right click, E, G), each with one job; the two
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. OpenWorld is played with keyboard and mouse, left hand on the keyboard and right hand on the mouse; there is no controller support. Keys can be changed in the Options (see rebinding keys ); this page describes the default bindings. There are four inputs for doing things to the things in the world, each with one job: Left click : the held thing's own use . A tool or weapon is swung (strike, chop, dig, hoe, draw water, light a fire); with an empty hand, your fist; anything else you hold (food, potions, clothes, letters) is used on yourself (eat, drink, put on, read). Right click : the held thing used on what you point at (sowing, feeding a cow, unlocking, roasting meat, and every kind of experiment the world has never seen). Holding a wall, a bed or the like builds it there. E : the hand . A thing lying loose on the ground is picked up; a thing set up is handled (talk, open a door, read a notice, sleep, pick a ripe crop). G : put . Put down, put in or put on top what you hold, or hand it to someone; whatever you put down lies loose and is never built. The other keys move, attack, cast skills, switch what you hold and open panels. s: Start here if you are playing OpenWorld for the first time: what the game is, the title page, how to
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. “What the world has never seen, it learns — and remembers.” — Trailer OpenWorld is a 2D pixel-art role-playing game you can play right in your browser. Every thing and every rule in the world is written code: chopping a tree drops wood, rain puts out burning things, and the undead roam at night. The player can do anything to anything. When you meet something the world has never defined, the world learns its result on the spot if an AI is connected, and remembers it forever; with no AI it is handled by default, and the game can still be played from start to finish. See The World Learns . The story takes place in The Lands of the Five Seals . The Seal-bearers of the Church of the Five Sufferings are weakening, and the nights grow longer year by year. The player wakes on Cloudtop at the mountain's top with a fairy called Lumi at their side, is drawn into the events of Firstlight Village on the way down, and sets out on the Pilgrim's Road. For the story see Main Story and Chapter 1 ; for a step-by-step walkthrough see Main Quest Walkthrough . Title page Behind the title page is the game's world itself, not a picture: the engine runs the world of a place live, its people walking about and working as they always do, under a camera that drifts slowly. Every ten seconds or so the picture fades through black to the next place, the six places of The Holy City in turn: Sunwell Abbey's front at dusk, the North Gate at dawn, the Bell Ward in the morning, the Market at its busiest, the Lamp War

x: Time in OpenWorld is always running: people keep to their schedules, monsters come out at night, and storms arrive on time. One minute of game time is one real second , an hour is one real minute, and a whole day is 24 real minutes. The date counts only the day, starting from Day 1, and the day changes at midnight, 00:00. The game has no weeks, seasons or years. See Seasons . The clock The wooden frame at the upper right of the screen is the clock: The first line is the date, such as “Day 3”. In the middle is a half-round dial, whose hand sweeps from 06:00 (left) through noon (top) to 02:00 (right); beside it is the weather icon. At the bottom is the time, which ticks over every 10 game minutes. In Chinese it is shown on the 24-hour clock (such as 21:30), in English on the 12-hour clock. s: Only the wrongs people see count: who did it (or what they looked like) is kept in each witness's me
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. Crime in OpenWorld works as in The Elder Scrolls: it counts only if someone sees it . If no one sees, what you stole is simply stolen; if someone does, they remember who did it, tell others, and the watch comes looking for you. These rules are the same for everyone: villagers steal too, and are seen by others and taken away by the guards too (see People's Needs ). Whose is it Whom a thing belongs to is decided in this order: It names its owner itself (for example the goods on Tobin 's wagon, or the bread in Hesper 's chest); otherwise, whose hands it is in: what a person carries is theirs; what is in a chest or cupboard belongs to the chest's owner; otherwise, where it lies: a thing on the step in front of a household's door belongs to that household. The house itself too: the walls you see from outside belong to whoever owns the rooms its door leads into (all but the door's cell), in the wild and in the cities alike. A household's things are shared by all of it: Marta , Mia , Pell and Lina are one household (the cook's family), Holt , Fennick and Oskar are one (the guards' house), Gus and Cass are one, and so on. When a thing is taken by someone who is not its owner, it still belongs to its owner : the stolen bread tucked in your bag is still Marta's. Only being handed to someone (as a gift, a sale, or giving it back) changes its owner. On merchants' shelves and in your bag, stolen things are marked “not yours”. Press E on someone else's thing lying loose on the ground or a table

s: OpenWorld has no energy (stamina) system; felling trees, mining and fighting cost no stamina, and th
x: OpenWorld has no energy (stamina) system . Felling trees, breaking stone, tilling and swinging weapons cost nothing at all; you can keep at them as long as you like, and you are never forced home to sleep because you are tired. The closest thing in the game is satiety : it falls slowly over time and has to be restored by eating; only at nine tenths or more does it heal you, and when it is empty you lose health. But satiety changes only with time, not with how much you do. The only limits on doing things back to back are their own cooldowns: at least 0.5 seconds between attacks, and a 4-second cooldown on Dash . Sleep only serves to skip the night, recover health and set your resting place ; see Sleeping . History 2026-10-01: An early version modeled on Stardew Valley had a stamina bar, with every use of a tool costing stamina. 2026-10-02: The team decided not to copy Stardew Valley's gameplay systems, and stamina was removed together with weeks, seasons and friendship points. Satiety was added the same day. x: Difficulty decides what happens after the player falls. When you start a new game you choose one of three, Easy, Normal or Hardcore; the default is Normal. Once chosen, difficulty cannot be changed, and it is kept with the save. Difficulty does not affect how strong monsters are, how fast you get hungry, or any other number; it only affects the price of death. The three difficulties Difficulty Description on the title page What you can do after falling Easy Get up where you fell, with everything Get up · Load a save · Title screen Normal (default) Respawn at your resting place; what you carried is bundled and left where you fell (the equipment you wear, the weapon in your hand and important items are not dropped); go back and press E on the bundle to take it all back Respawn · Load a save · Title screen Hardcore One life Only Title screen; this save ends here Old saves with no difficulty recorded are treated as Normal. The tutorial and the Boss Challenge have no difficulty to choose, and falling in the tutorial is treated as Normal. Falling When the player's health drops to 0, the character collapses ( down ) and the whole world stops: The screen is washed with red, with “You died!” in the middle. Below it is what felled you, for example “Felled by bat”; when it cannot be found out, it says “You fell”. Below that are the buttons the difficulty allows. The death screen takes only mouse clicks on its buttons. What can make the player fall: attacks, burning, bleeding, falls (6 points for every storey beyond the first) and so on. s: What music plays when — the title's, a scene's, a boss fight's by its phase, a fight's, each place's
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. The music follows what is happening in the game: a map does not loop one piece for ever. In the wilds a piece plays and then falls silent for a while, leaving only the ambience : the wind, the rain, running water, a fire, birds by day and crickets by night. The ambience is made as you play; there are no recordings behind it. What plays when From the top down, the first that holds decides: When What plays The title screen the title's own piece, whatever place shows behind it A scene the music the scene asks for, or silence, until the scene ends A boss fight that boss's own fight music; the White Knight Alberic changes to another at his second phase A fight the moment something comes at you, or you strike someone, the fight music cuts in; after the fight it plays on for 7 seconds, then fades back to what was playing Otherwise the place's music, in its version for the hour and the weather While a fight, a scene or a boss plays over a place's music, the place's piece is only held, and goes on afterwards from where it stopped. While you lie fallen (see Difficulty ) the music stops; only the fall's jingle sounds. s: The ten drumsticks at the upper right of the toolbar: satiety falls in two stages, quickly while you
x: Satiety is shown as ten drumsticks at the upper right of the toolbar, mirroring the hearts on the left. The maximum is 20, 2 points per drumstick, drawn in halves and emptying from left to right. Hover over the drumsticks to see “Satiety current / 20”. Satiety falls over time and is restored by eating. Well fed, you heal; hungry down to 0, you lose health. A new game starts with 12 satiety, exactly six tenths. How fast it falls Satiety falls in two stages, counted in game time (1 game minute = 1 real second): State Condition Per point lost Full Six tenths or more (12 or more) 48 game minutes hungry Below six tenths (under 12) 6 game hours (7.5 times slower) asleep While sleeping in a bed Another 4 times slower, multiplied with “hungry” After a full meal it takes about six and a half game hours to fall to six tenths, just in time for the next meal. Eat two or three meals a normal day and you stay above six tenths. Below six tenths you become hungry and satiety falls very slowly: from six tenths to 0 takes about 3 game days. Skipping meals, from full to empty takes about 3 game days. Eat back above six tenths and “hungry” goes away. Over a whole night's sleep, someone well fed loses only two or three points. Eating Hold the food in your hand (select its slot on the toolbar). Left-click (using it on yourself) and confirm “Eat X?”. Pointing the mouse at yourself and right-clicking does the same. s: How a page file is written: the front matter, links, templates, and the fixed structure of each kind
x: “The basic format and wording of content of the same kind should be kept consistent.” — This wiki follows the editing conventions of the Stardew Valley Wiki This page explains how a page file is written, for the English edition. If you have not read Editing Basics yet, read that page first: its last section explains how an English page follows its Chinese one. Where files go Every English page is a Markdown file under wiki/en/pages/ , at the same path, with the same Chinese file name, as the Chinese page it translates: wiki/pages/人物/伊尔丝修女.md is translated by wiki/en/pages/人物/伊尔丝修女.md . The two are paired by their path, not by their titles, so an English file is never renamed or moved on its own. The subfolders only sort the files and do not affect the address. The address depends only on the English title: /wiki/en/Sister_Ilse , with spaces written as _ . The English title is the title: in the front matter, or, for a page about a game thing, the game's English name. Titles are unique across the edition; if two pages end up with the same title, the build reports an error. Front matter The very top of the file is a few lines of "key: value", between two --- lines: --- summary: The keeper of the fire in Firstlight Village's chapel. categories: Firstlight Village aliases: Ilse source: 3f9a1c0b7d2e --- Key Required Description title For a page not about a game thing The page's English title. A page about a game thing (a person, an item, a monster, a location, a quest…) takes the game's English name as its title, and a title: there is ignored. summary Recommended One sentence, us

s: Edit a page in three steps; create a page; discuss big changes first; preview locally; how the Engli
x: Welcome to editing the OpenWorld Wiki. The wiki is written in Chinese first: the Chinese pages are the source, and this English edition is their translation. Every page is a file in the GitHub repository SihanXU/symbolic-world : a Chinese page lives under wiki/pages/ , its English translation under wiki/en/pages/ at the same path. Everyone on the project team can edit them. A minute or two after a change is merged into the main branch (main), the site updates by itself. This page is about editing the English pages. How the English edition follows the Chinese one is explained in full in the last section, The English edition . Editing a page Open the page on the site and click "Edit" at the top right. You land on GitHub's editor for this file (you need to be signed in to GitHub and be a collaborator on the repository). If the page has not been translated yet, the button says "Translate" instead: it starts the English file on GitHub with the Chinese text already in it, ready to be translated (see The English edition ). Edit the text. For the format, see Format Manual ; for how to write, see Style Guide . At the bottom of the page, write one line saying what you changed, then: Small changes (a typo, a missing sentence, a wrong number, a better wording): choose "Commit directly to the main branch" and commit. Big changes (rewriting a section, changing the structure, a whole new translation): choose "Create a new branch … and start a pull request", and wait for someone to look at it before it is merged. After you commit, the repository's automatic check builds the whole wiki, bot

s: How to write: an encyclopedia's voice, facts only, the game's own names, a source for every fact, an
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. This wiki is OpenWorld's encyclopedia, and also the game's design proposal: what the game already has is described as it is now; what is decided but not built is marked "Planned"; what is not decided yet is marked "To be designed". The English edition is a translation of the Chinese one, which is the source. Everything below holds for what a page says in either edition; a few sections add a note on translating. How a translation is written: Translate faithfully and fully. Everything a reader reads, the same paragraphs, lists, tables and notes, with nothing summarized, dropped or added. An English page says what its Chinese page says. Keep the headings one for one with the Chinese page : the same number of headings, at the same levels, in the same order. The two editions match sections by their position, so a heading added, dropped or moved breaks every link into the page's sections. Leave the code alone. Inline code , code blocks, ids, file paths, numbers and keys stay exactly as they are. Links and templates. A link target or a template argument may stay as the Chinese page has it; npm run wiki:translate -- relink file rewrites them into English (see Editing Basics ). Translate the free text of a template: a quotation and its speaker, a spoiler's title, an image's caption, the text of {{planned|…}} and {{tbd|…}} . The game's lines. x: Trophies are the gear monsters drop. Every kind of monster has one trophy piece that belongs to it (one piece, not a set). Each time you fell one, there is a chance that piece appears straight in the bag of whoever felled it. Rules Who gets it : whoever fells it (the last blow). The piece never lands on the ground; it goes straight into the bag, while an icon flies into the bag on screen; when the player gets one, the lower left says “A trophy: X!”. Drop rate : 4% for each ordinary monster, 10% for the stronger ones, and certain for the boss-like monsters ( Slime King , cyclops , the dragon of Cinder Peak , barrow warden ). Pity : if 49 of one kind of monster are felled in a row without the piece dropping, the 50th surely drops it. Each person keeps their own count for each kind of monster; once it drops, the count for that kind starts over. Main stats come from the level : every trophy has its own level (the stronger the monster, the higher the level), and its defense and attack are worked out from the level, not from its material or quality : a piece of a set counts as Fine (×1.25), a standalone piece as Masterwork (×1.5). Random affixes : when it drops it rolls 4 affixes all the same, so the same trophy is different every time it drops. Only from monsters : it cannot be forged , and no merchant sells it. Tooltip : hover over it and it reads “✧ Trophy · dropped by X”. Each monster's page names its trophy and drop rate in its “Drops” section. x: A set is a few pieces of gear that belong together. The more pieces of one set you wear, the more bonuses you gain on top. The game's sets come from two sources: the outfit each profession forges at an anvil , and the trophies of one family of monsters. Rules Sets follow those of Dungeon & Fighter (DNF), and come in two kinds: Set Pieces Slots Bonus tiers Armor set 6 Head, shoulders, body, hands, belt, feet At 2, 4 and 6 pieces worn Trinket set 3 Necklace, earring, ring At 2 and 3 pieces worn Pieces are counted by slot : of one set, each slot counts only once. Wear a ring of the same set on each hand and it counts as 1 piece. Bonuses add up : with 4 pieces worn, you have the bonuses of both the 2-piece and the 4-piece tier. The main hand and off hand are in no set : weapons and off-hand pieces stand alone, with only their own numbers. Only what is worn counts; what sits in the bag does not. Hover over a piece of a set and the bottom of the tooltip says “◆ Set name Set (pieces worn/total pieces)”, with one tier of bonuses on each line below: green for tiers reached, grey for those not yet. s: Minor monsters have moves of their own too: the cells about to be struck light up on the ground firs
x: Besides its plain attack, every kind of monster has a skill or two of its own: slimes hop next to you, wolves lunge along a straight line, boars lower their heads and charge, cave spiders spit webs to bind you… As with bosses , a monster marks the cells it will strike on the ground before the move, and the blow lands a moment later, so every move can be dodged. How to tell a move is coming The move's name rises over its head , such as “Lunge” or “Web Spit”. Marks light up on the ground : the marked cells are the cells that will be struck, and the color deepens as the blow draws near. Red : damage. Purple : control, such as webbed, Mired, stunned. Amber : calling companions or strengthening itself, such as Howl or Shell Up. These moves mark no cells. The monster takes a stance : one about to leap squashes down, one about to charge draws back, one about to smash all round puffs up, a caster sways side to side, one about to howl rears up trembling. The fuller the stance, the nearer the blow. The monster flashes white : the wind-up is nearly over, and the blow is about to land. Listen : casting and howling make a sound as they begin; leaps, charges and smashes make one as they land. The marks are fixed the moment the move begins: walk away and it still strikes the cells it marked. How to answer Step out of the marks. Step one cell sideways and the straight-line moves (Lunge, Charge, Bone Toss, Swoop) miss. Interrupt it. They lie where it fell and are not drawn to you by themselves; press E to pick them up. The amount is half of the materials in its body (at least 1), by the same rule as breaking a stone or felling a tree (see Durability and Breaking ). s: The few small bonuses a piece of gear rolls at random when it is “born” (2 to 6, by its quality): th
x: Affixes are the random small bonuses on a piece of gear. A piece's numbers come in two parts: its main stats come from its form, material , quality and level (a monster trophy 's main stats are worked out from its level); its affixes are rolled the moment it is made, so no two pieces of the same thing are alike. What gear has affixes Things that can be worn or held in the main hand (weapons, armor, clothing, trinkets, off-hand pieces) roll affixes when they are “born”: forged at an anvil , or crafted (by hand or beside a workbench alike); the trophies monsters drop; the goods merchants restock every morning (see Trading ); gear laid out on a map. A thing that already carries affixes never rolls again. The only gear without affixes is the starting weapon handed out when you choose a profession . Named gear from quests rolls too (fixed by its name, the same in every game). How they are rolled How many a piece rolls depends on its quality : Crude 2, Common 3, Fine 4, Masterwork 5, Vowbound 5, Stigmatic 6; a monster trophy always 4. No two are the same. Its moves are the same thing as monster skills : the cells to be struck are marked on the ground first (the wind-up), and the blow lands a moment later; stand outside the marks and it cannot hit you. x: Legendary Arms are the weapons that belong to the four professions , two to each, of Stigmatic quality, each with a power of its own. They never lie on the ground and cannot be crafted: when a Seal-bearer falls, he leaves one Legendary weapon belonging to the profession of whoever felled him. How to obtain When you defeat a Seal-bearer after choosing a profession, he drops a Legendary weapon of your profession, plus 4 Iron Ore . The one dropped is the first of the profession's two that has not yet appeared in the world. Each Legendary weapon appears only once in a world. If you have not chosen a profession, the Seal-bearer drops only Iron Ore. At present the game holds only the first Seal-bearer, The White Knight Alberic , so each profession can obtain only its first weapon: the Assassin's Nightfang, the Warrior's Oathbrand, the Ranger's Galestring and the Mage's Emberheart. The second ones wait for later Seal-bearers. Nothing obtained in the Boss Challenge is saved. s: What the Lands of the Five Seals and the Holy City each make: every region's own full set of gear an
x: Regional goods are the things each region of the continent makes and sells itself. All of them are variants of some base item: a “Fenland Sword” handles just like a Sword , a “Smoked Herring” eats just like Grilled Fish — the world's rules for them are exactly those for the original; what differs is the name, the icon, the substance , the worth, and where they can be found. Each region has three kinds: Gear and tools made locally : a full set of weapons, armour, clothes, tools and jewelry that the local smiths, tailors and jewelers make in their own style (“Frostfang Sword”, “Redmarch Pauldrons”, “Hallowed Ring”), from the substances produced there. Local goods : things found only there — the Whaling Harpoon and Stockfish of Frostfang Coast , the Chaff Bread and Loaded Dice of The Vale of Scales , the Mourning Veil and Jellied Eel of The Pale Fens . Famous pieces : a region's renowned craft, rare and dear (three times the price of the original); famous gear is always of Fine quality. They are not placed on the playable maps but in each region's places not yet open : the chests and storage barrels at every household's door, the shops' shelves, the smithies' weapon chests, the inns' casks, the temples' candlesticks and bookshelves, the camps' crates, the market stalls, and the chests deep in ruins and caves. A place mostly keeps its own region's things; to the Holy City pilgrims come from every quarter, and goods of other regions can be found there too. Across the whole continent, more than twenty thousand things are kept this way. Goods by region Frostfang Coast (146 kinds)

s: What things are made of: wood, stone, iron, steel, silver… The substance sets the multipliers of pow
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. Substance is what a thing is made of: wood, stone, iron, steel, silver, leather, cloth… The same form (a “sword”, say) can be made of different substances; the substance is written into the name (“Iron Sword”, “Silver Sword”) and also decides how strong and how hard it is. “ Materials ” are a category of items (logs, stones…); “substance” is what a thing is made of. A Plank is a material; its substance is wood. What the substance decides Power and defense : each substance has an attack multiplier and a defense multiplier. A weapon's power = the form's power × the substance's attack multiplier × the quality 's multiplier × the level 's multiplier; an armour piece's defense likewise. Hardness : a tool or weapon softer than its target does nothing to it, and says “Too hard.” A fist cannot break stone, for example, and a wooden thing cannot cut rock. Class : substances fall into the classes wood, plant, stone, ore, metal, earth, fiber, hide, bone, organic, flesh and crystal. Tools work at a different efficiency on each class; see the efficiency table below. Traits : wood, leather, cloth and silk burn; metal conducts, and lightning electrifies it; crystal, glass, clay and obsidian are brittle, and the earth element can shatter them. See Elements . What substance crafted things are made of A thing you make takes the substance of its main material: an axe made from stone is a Stone Axe, a shield made from planks a Wooden Shield, a bow made from sticks a Wooden Bow. x: Firecracker Category Miscellany Chinese name 爆竹 ID item/misc/firework The Firecracker is a string of paper-rolled crackers. It cannot be obtained in normal play: none lies on any map, it cannot be crafted , and no quest gives one. Source There is no set way to get it in the game yet. Uses The game data records no set use for it. Right-click something else while holding it, and the world may learn a new use (see The World Learns ). The tooltip says the Firecracker “Goes off when it catches fire”. Going off : a Firecracker is made of paper and goes off the moment it catches fire: everything in the four tiles directly next to it, above, below, left and right (people, creatures, walls, furniture…), takes a fire blow of power 1 (less defense, at least 1); anything flammable and not wet in those tiles catches fire, and the Firecracker itself is gone, leaving no Ash . Its own tile and the diagonal tiles are not hit. How to light it : left-click the Firecracker on the ground with a fire source such as a Torch ; throw it into a lit campfire ; or let fire reach it (spreading fire, a blow carrying the fire element). A wet Firecracker touched by fire is only dried. Whoever lights it standing right next to it is also hit and catches fire; lighting it from a diagonal tile is safe. The blast has only an eighth of the force of a Blackpowder Bomb . See Fire . History 2026-09-30: Added to the game's item catalogue. 2026-10-08: It goes off when it catches fire, instead of only burning to ash. s: A blackpowder bomb; it bursts as soon as it catches fire, dealing a fire blow of force 8 to the four
x: Blackpowder Bomb Category Miscellany Chinese name 黑火药炸弹 ID item/misc/bomb The Blackpowder Bomb is a bomb packed with blackpowder. It cannot be obtained in normal play: it is not placed on any map, cannot be crafted , and no quest gives it. Source There is no set way to get it in the game yet. Uses The game data records no set use for it. Right-click something else while holding it, and the world may learn a new use (see The World Learns ). The tooltip says the bomb “bursts when it catches fire”. Bursting : the bomb bursts the moment it catches fire. Everything in the four tiles directly above, below, left and right of it (people, creatures, walls, furniture…) takes a fire blow of force 8 (minus defense); anything in those tiles that can burn and is not wet is set alight; the bomb itself is gone and leaves no Ash . Creatures and people caught in the blast also catch fire. Its own tile and the diagonal tiles are not hit. How to light it : left-click the bomb on the ground with a fire source such as a Torch ; throw it into a lit campfire ; or let fire reach it (spreading fire, a blow carrying the fire element). A wet bomb touched by fire is only dried. Whoever lights it standing right beside it is caught in the blast too; lighting it from a diagonal tile is safe. It is eight times as strong as a Firecracker . The other thing that bursts into flame is something soaked in oil; see Flask of Oil and oil . History 2026-09-30: Added to the game's item catalogue. 2026-10-08: Bursts when it catches fire, instead of just burning to ash. Items Weapons Sword • Dagger • Axe • Dragonsbane

s: Items held in the hand to attack with: profession weapons and common weapons, attack range, elements
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. A weapon is an item held in the hand to attack with. Hold a weapon and left-click a target, or press Space to attack in front of you: that is one blow. Attack power = your own attack + the weapon's power. For the rules of fighting see Combat . Profession weapons and common weapons Some weapons belong to a single profession . Others can hold them, store them and give them away, but cannot attack with them; they are told “Only an X can fight with a Y”. Profession Profession weapons Assassin Dagger Warrior Sword , Scimitar , and the off-hand Shield Ranger Bow Mage Staff The other weapons are common weapons that anyone can use: Axe , Club , Mace , Warhammer , Spear , Halberd , Wand , Dragonsbane . A profession's talents work only on that profession's weapons; the tooltip of a common weapon says “Common weapon: no profession talent bonus”. Before you have chosen a profession (which waits until level 5), only common weapons can be used to fight. When you first choose a profession you get a starting weapon: an Iron Dagger for the Assassin, an Iron Sword and a Wooden Shield for the Warrior, a Wooden Bow for the Ranger, a Wooden Staff for the Mage. Attack range How far a left-click attack reaches depends on the weapon in your hand: Weapon Range Most weapons, bare hands 1 tile Spear , Halberd 2 tiles Staff 4 tiles Wand 5 tiles Bow 6 tiles A ranged attack can only go out along your own row or column. Bows, wands and staves fire a projectile in the direction you face. Some skills and Legendar

s: Things that can be planted in farmland: where to get seeds, how to sow them, and the full table of e
x: Seeds are items that can be planted in farmland. Sow them and water them, and the crop grows stage by stage; once ripe, a harvest gives back seeds as well as the crop. For the rules of farming see Farming ; for each crop see Crops . Sowing Turn grass, dirt, sand or snow into farmland with a Hoe . Hold the seeds and right-click an empty tile of farmland to plant a “sprout”. The fourteen vegetables can also be chosen as “Sow X” on the “Farming” page of build mode ( B ). Water it by left-clicking it with a container holding water. A watered crop grows one stage two game hours later: sprout → young plant → ripe. Each stage needs one watering. Crops grow only in the open; those under a roof do not grow. Once ripe, reap it with a Sickle for 2 portions of crop and 2 of seed; a fertilized crop (with Ash or Fertilizer ) gives 1 more portion of crop. You can also press E to pick one portion of crop and one of seed by hand. Tomatoes , corn , blueberries , strawberries , hot peppers , eggplants and berry bushes grow fruit again after a harvest, with no need to replant. Crops do not wither, and there are no seasons. Where to get them The vegetable garden in Firstlight Village : the tool crate by the garden (“Garden Supplies”) holds 2 each of Carrot Seeds , Turnip Seeds , Tomato Seeds and Pumpkin Seeds , plus a hoe, a sickle, a smith hammer and a bucket of water. The garden already grows these four crops at every stage. The trading stall at The Held Ground : its “Farming” page sells the seeds of the fourteen vegetables, plus Wheat Seeds, Herb Seeds, Berry Seeds and acorns, for Dawnmarks

Right-click something else while holding it, and the world may learn a new use (see The World Learns ). Storing and taking : E opens or closes it; while it is open, G puts the thing in your hand into it, up to 40 things; opening it shows the chest panel, where clicking a thing moves it between the storehouse and your bag (see Chests and Containers ). Rooms : a room with 3 or more containers is a storeroom (no effect for now). Fire : it is wooden and can catch fire, burning down to a portion of Ash ; what is inside drops on the spot. Its material is bedrock (hardness 9), harder than any tool: whatever you strike it with only raises a puff of dust and the message “Bare rock. Growing back It carries a timer of one game day (24 game hours, about 24 minutes of real time). When the time is up, it turns back into a coal seam in place, at full durability, and mining it again gives 2 more Coal . The timer keeps running while you are off the map and catches up when you come back. See Mining . History 2026-10-14: Added. Before this, a vein simply vanished when mined out, and only the Old Mine grew new ones at random elsewhere. Log pile Category Nature Chinese name 柴堆 ID fixture/nature/logpile The log pile (natural object) is the class of natural objects that are wood stacked into a pile. It never appears on a map by itself; every log pile in the game is a kind of it: the single firewood stack west of the tent in the camp at the Ford . Press E to open the stall panel and buy seeds, fertilizer, a shovel, feed, buckets, crated livestock, bait and a fishing rod with Dawnmarks , or sell it what you grow, raise and catch in exchange for Dawnmarks. This opens the stall page of the menu, with four shelves: Farming , Ranching , Fishing and Sell , and above them how many Dawnmarks you carry. Lamp post Category Light sources Chinese name 路灯 ID fixture/light/lamppost A lamp post is a metal post with a lamp burning at the top. Firstlight Village and Emberfall have two each, lit from the start. Like every lit fire, it keeps monsters away and lights up its surroundings at night. Source Placed on maps: Firstlight Village ×4, Emberfall ×2 Two in Firstlight Village: one on the east side of the square, one on the west side of the village. Two in Emberfall, near the square. You cannot make one. Uses The game data records no set use for it. Right-click something else while holding it, and the world may learn a new use (see The World Learns ). Monsters keep away Except fire monsters, monsters do not come within 2 tiles of anything lit or burning, nor chase a person standing there (see Factions and Temper ). At night, people and creatures standing within 3 tiles of a lit fire see as far as by day. On screen a ring of warm light surrounds a lamp post (see Day and Night ). Lighting and putting out Putting out : holding a container full of water, left-click it and the lamp goes out. Rain does not put out a lit lamp post. Lighting : holding a Torch , left-click it, or hit it with the fire element. Once you have learned Firemaker , right-clicking it holding an ordinary stick lights it too. When it is wet, the first touch of fire only dries it. Once lit it stays lit, with no need to add oil. Warming yourself Press E with empty hands at a lit lamp post (“Warm yourself at the lamp post”):

s: Gear worn on the head, body, hands, feet and off hand: how defense is counted, how to put it on, and
x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. Armour is gear worn on the body that adds defense, filling five slots: head, body, hands, feet and off hand. For gear in the other five slots (earrings, necklaces, shoulders, belts and rings) see Accessories . The equipment slots number eleven in all; see Equipment . How defense is counted A piece of armour's defense = the form's defense × the material 's multiplier × the quality 's multiplier. For example, among helmets an iron one is harder than a leather one, and a Fine one harder than a Common one. The defense of everything you wear is added together. When you are attacked, the damage is reduced by your defense, but at least 1 point always remains. Clothing (hats, boots, gloves) has no defense of its own, except the named pieces. Armour does not wear out, there is no repairing, and there are no set bonuses. Putting it on Hold it in your hand and left-click to use it on yourself, and you put it on. You can also click the figure's equipment slots in the pack ( I ), or right-click an item and choose “Equip”. Only one piece can be worn in each slot. Gear exclusive to a profession works only for that profession: only a Warrior can wear a shield in the off hand. Eating Hold the food in your hand and left-click to use it on yourself; you are asked “Eat X?”, and confirming eats it. Eating restores only satiety, not health directly. With satiety at 90% or more, health slowly recovers by itself. See Satiety and Health . Herbs are the exception: they can be eaten and also restore a little health. Raw food does no harm when eaten; it is just less filling than cooked. Food does not spoil. Skills can make food more filling or make satiety drop more slowly; see Skills . Drinking Hold a potion or drink in your hand and left-click to use it on yourself; you are asked “Drink X?”, and drinking it restores health. A Healing Potion restores the most; Wine Bottle , Mug of Ale , Antidote and Murky Potion restore less. A Bucket , Empty Flask or Empty Waterskin holding water can be drunk too, restoring 2 health; the container is left behind empty. A Bucket of Milk restores both 4 health and 4 satiety; once drunk, the bucket is left behind empty. Buckets, flasks and waterskins are tools: their left click fills them with water, waters or splashes; to drink what is in one, hold it and right-click yourself. x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. Woodcutting is chopping trees with an axe. A felled tree leaves a stump, two Log , one Stick , and sometimes an Acorn . Logs split into Plank , and planks are the material most used in building and crafting . Chopping a tree Hold an axe ( Axe ), point the mouse at a tree (a tree or a pine tree) and press the left button. The prompt bar at the top reads “Chop …”, and the tree's cell is outlined. Every chop takes some durability off the tree and leaves an axe mark on it (status notched ). The mark lasts 10 seconds. If you do not chop again within 10 seconds, the tree heals and its durability is full again. A tree has 10 durability. Each chop deals your own attack plus the axe's power, and an axe's efficiency against wood is 1 (see Durability and Breaking ). A new player has attack 2 and a stone axe has power 5, so a chop does 7 points: two chops fell a tree . When the tree falls you see “The tree falls!”, it turns into a stump where it stood, and it drops 2 logs and 1 stick, with a 25% chance of 1 acorn as well. With Woodcutter learned, every tree drops 1 more log. After you learn it, trees no longer drop acorns. What drops pops out onto the ground; walk close and it flies into your bag. Without an axe Bare hands : a punch on a tree does 1 damage, so ten punches fell a tree. Fists leave no axe mark, so the durability you knock off never grows back. s: The six elements, fire, water, ice, lightning, wind and earth, and how each reacts with what it touc
x: The game has six elements: fire, water, ice, lightning, wind and earth. An element reacts with what it touches: fire sets hay alight, water puts fire out, ice freezes a wet slime, lightning runs across wet ground. These reactions are all rules, and they treat the player, residents, monsters, items and the ground alike. The six elements Element Weapon affix Code fire of Embers fire water of Tides water ice of Frost ice lightning of Storms lightning wind of Gales wind earth of Stone earth A weapon or staff that carries an element has the element's title in its name: of Embers (fire), of Tides (water), of Frost (ice), of Storms (lightning), of Gales (wind), of Stone (earth). Where elements come from Weapons : a weapon, staff or wand with an element puts its element on whoever it hits (the blow's own damage still counts). Creatures : some monsters carry an element of their own, and their attacks carry it: fire slime , fire imp , dragon whelp , the dragon of Cinder Peak (fire); frost slime , frost wolf , ghost (ice); stone golem (earth); and others. Torches, flint and steel, candles : hold one and left-click a thing, and you touch it with fire. Water : a full bucket, flask or waterskin; left-click a thing to splash water on it. Weather : rain is water without force, falling on people, creatures and burning things in the open; in a thunderstorm a bolt of lightning strikes every so often (see Weather ). The ground : stepping into mud gets you wet; a burning thing sets alight what touches it; electrified ground shocks whoever stands on it. Fire Touches Result Something oiled Explod

s: Hoe, sow, water, harvest: each stage of a crop takes one to four game hours, as the seed's descripti
x: Farming is growing crops in farmland: hoe the ground into farmland, sow seeds, water once per stage, and harvest when ripe. The vegetables you harvest can be eaten and bring back seeds; a surplus can be sold at the trading stall on The Held Ground . What you can grow is in Crops . The first time you walk into the vegetable garden in Firstlight Village , Lumi begins the guide quest A Lesson in the Garden , which takes you through it all, from the toolbox to cutting, sowing and watering. A plot from start to finish Hoe : hold a Hoe and left-click a cell of grass, dirt, sand or snow; it becomes farmland. Sow : hold seeds and right-click an empty cell of farmland (“Sow …”). The seed becomes a “… sprout”. Water : hold a container full of water and left-click the crop: “You water the ….” The container is emptied, and the crop gets watered . Wait : 1, 2 or 4 game hours depending on the kind, as the seed's and the crop's tooltips say. A crop grows one stage only if it is in the open and has water: sprout → young plant → ripe. Water again : an ordinary watering serves only one stage, so the young plant needs watering again. Once you have learned Irrigation , one watering serves two stages in a row, each at the same speed. Harvest : once it is ripe, hold a Sickle and left-click to cut it, or press E to pick it by hand. From sowing to ripe, turnips, parsnips and radishes take as little as 2 game hours; pumpkins, cauliflowers, melons, corn and blueberries take 8 hours; the rest 4 hours. The panel lists every recipe in the game; nothing has to be unlocked, and when you have the materials you can make it. It is not called “combining”. Where recipes come from Everything that can be made says two things: what it is made of, and where it is made. The recipe comes from these two; there is no separate recipe table: Made of : a stone axe is 1 stone, 1 stick and 1 cut grass; a wall is 2 planks. Where it is made : “by hand” is made anywhere, any time — that is this panel; “forge” and “anvil” recipes are made by pressing E on that thing to open its own panel (see Smithing ). They wander about on the grass and never attack anyone; when hit, they run. Feed them Animal Feed or Wheat and they are fed . A fed cow can be milked with an empty Bucket for a Bucket of Milk . Two fed animals of the same kind side by side bring forth a young one; the young one grows up after a while. A chicken lays an Egg every 3 game hours, fed or not. The trading stall on The Held Ground sells feed, buckets, and hens and calves in crates, and buys eggs and milk. There is no shearing, no barns, no penning with fences and no taming; there are no Animal Husbandry skills either.
