s: Press B for Building mode: place walls, floors, doors, stairs, beds and workbenches; build campfires
x: Building is putting a thing into a cell of the world: a wall, a floor, a bed, a campfire. The usual way is Building mode: press B to open the building panel (its title reads “BUILD MODE”), choose a thing, point at a cell beside you, and press the left button or E to put it there. You can build a house without Building mode too: hold a wall you have made and right-click a cell to build it in that cell, or hold the right button and drag to build a row. This is the same thing that Building mode puts down. Pressing G only puts it on the ground: a wall or bed put down that way lies loose there like any ordinary thing and is not built (press E to pick it up again). See Placing from your hand . For houses of several storeys, how walls stack, ceilings and stairs, see Storeys . For when a house counts as a room, see Rooms . Placing from your hand Walls, floors, doors, stairs, beds, workbenches and the like are in your bag once made, and you can place them straight from your hand: Right-click an empty cell beside you, a floor, or something already built (a wall on a wall, a floor on a wall), and it is built there. Hold the right button and drag , and one is built in every cell the mouse passes; it does nothing where it passes trees, water or people. A translucent preview under the mouse shows exactly where it will be drawn once built, and how big. Holding a floor, press R and the right click lays a ceiling instead; press it again to switch back. You can also Alt+right-click and choose “Ceiling” among the levels listed. Things with a direction ( stairs , fences ) are built facing the

s: A space closed in on every side and covered overhead is a room; what is inside decides whether it is
x: The game recognizes rooms by itself: a space closed in by walls on every side and covered overhead is a room. You need not place anything special to “designate” it. What is inside decides what kind of room it is: one with a bed is a bedroom, one with a fire a kitchen. What counts as a room A set of cells is a room when all of these hold: On the same storey , every cell can be stood on (there is a floor or ground underfoot, and nothing solid such as a wall in its space slot). Every cell is covered overhead : the same cell on the storey above has a floor or a wall (see Storeys ). The cell with the stairs counts as covered: that is the way up. Closed in on every side : walking out from any cell inside, you meet a wall or a door; you cannot reach an uncovered place, nor the edge of the map. No more than 256 cells. Anything larger counts as outdoors. A door, open or shut, is an edge just like a wall, so a house is a room without the door being shut. Nor does it need a door at all: cells walled in on four sides that no one can walk into count as a room too. On maps that are not outdoors, such as caves and chapels, everywhere counts as covered. Room uses The things inside give a room its uses. A room can have several uses at once. s: Houses can be built upward: how walls, floors, ceilings, stairs and doors are placed, what holds up
x: A house can be built several storeys high. Every storey is made of the same few things: the floor underfoot, the walls and furniture on that storey, and the ceiling overhead. You go upstairs by Stairs . This page covers how the storeys are put together and what holds up what; how to place things is in Building , and when a house counts as a room is in Rooms . What a storey is Above the ground storey you can build up to 4 more storeys . The view is top-down and slanted: one storey is drawn one cell high. So things on the second storey are drawn one cell higher than the cell they are in, and things on the third storey two cells higher. A cell has two slots on every storey: The floor slot : what you stand on. On the ground storey the floor slot is the terrain itself (grass, dirt…), which you can cover with a floor laid on top. Upstairs the floor slot either has a floor laid or is empty (open air). The space slot : the one solid upright thing on that storey, at most one: a wall, a door, a flight of stairs, a chest, a workbench, a campfire. Beds, people and loose items do not take this slot (a person cannot share a cell with something solid). The ceiling of one storey is the floor of the storey above. The same planks are a ceiling from below and a floor from above. Each storey builds only its own storey Someone standing on a storey can reach only three things: the floor slot of their own storey, the space slot of their own storey, and the ceiling overhead. s: Stand on a bed and press E to sleep until 6 in the morning: time speeds ahead, health comes back and
x: To sleep, stand on a bed and press E . Once you lie down, time speeds ahead to 6:00 in the morning, and you wake with some of your health restored. A bed you have slept in becomes your rest point : on Normal difficulty, when you fall you get back up here. The game has no stamina (see Energy ), so sleep is not required; it is the way to pass the night, recover health and set your rest point. How to sleep You have to stand on a bed to reach it: walk onto the bed and press E ; the prompt is “Sleep”. “You lie down.” Time immediately speeds ahead to 6:00 in the morning. You can sleep at any time: lie down at 22:00 and you sleep 8 game hours; lie down at 7 in the morning and you sleep until 6 the next day. While asleep you have the asleep status and cannot move. The game has no bed lying ready; you make your own: 2 planks and 2 cut grass (the “wooden bed” in Crafting ), or place one directly in Building mode. A bed can be carried: knock it with an axe, pickaxe or hammer (left click) and it comes loose whole where it stood; press E to pick it up (close by, it is drawn into your bag by itself); when you get where you are going, hold it and right-click a cell, and it is set up for sleeping. When you wake Health restored : your missing health × the rest value, rounded up. The bed is in a bedroom (a bed inside a house closed in on every side and covered overhead): rest value 1, everything you were missing is restored. “You sleep deeply and wake refreshed.” The bed is anywhere else: rest value 0.5, half is restored. “You get some sleep, after a fashion.” Rest point : this bed becomes y

s: Everything that can be broken has durability; how much a blow knocks off depends on the tool's effic
x: Everything in the world that can be broken has durability: a tree, a rock, a wall, a chest; a creature's durability is its health. How much durability a blow knocks off depends on what is struck and what it is struck with. When durability reaches 0, the thing breaks: a tree falls, a rock splits, a chest comes apart into planks, a creature falls. The ground itself cannot be broken: the terrain laid at the very bottom, such as grass, dirt and water, has no durability. How much one blow knocks off Striking with something (the left button, or Space to strike ahead) is called a “blow”. A blow uses the weapon or tool in your hand; with empty hands (and likewise when you strike with Space while holding something else) it uses the weapon in your main hand, and failing that your own body: a punch. Pressing the left button with anything else in hand is not a blow; it uses that thing on yourself. Force = your own attack + the power of what is in your hand. The player starts with attack 2; a stone axe has power 5, so one chop is 7. Too hard? If the material of what is in your hand is softer than the target, nothing comes off, and you see only “Too hard.”. Efficiency : force is multiplied by efficiency. Efficiency depends on what use the thing in your hand has (axe, pick, shovel, hammer) or what edge (cut, blunt, pierce, dig, magic), against what material the target is. When a thing has several uses and edges, the best one counts. Defense : the target's defense is subtracted, with at least 1 knocked off. Creatures also have dodging, blocking and so on; see Combat . x: The Chinese page has changed since this translation was made: some of this may be out of date. Mining is breaking stony things with a pickaxe ( Pickaxe ). Rocks and boulders give Stone ; ore veins give Iron Ore , Coal and Gold Ore . The mining ground you can reach in Chapter 1 is Dawn Hill Mine on the west slope of Dawn Hill , north of Firstlight Village (iron and coal, with a stone pickaxe at the entrance); later there are The Old Mine and the Quarry on The Held Ground . Stones grow on the ground by themselves anyway (see Foraging ); mining is a bigger, faster source of stone, and one of the only sources of iron ore. Veins grow back : break open a vein and it drops 2 ore, leaving a spent face where it stood — bedrock that no tool can touch — which turns back into a vein after one game day (24 game hours, about 24 minutes), in the same place. The clock keeps running while you are off that map. Boulders and rocks are gone once broken. How to mine Hold a pickaxe, point the mouse at a rock and press the left button. The prompt bar at the top reads “Mine …”, and the rock's cell is outlined. Each blow deals your own attack plus the pickaxe's power. A pickaxe's efficiency against both stone and ore is 1. A new player has attack 2 and a stone pickaxe has power 4, so a blow does 6 points. When durability reaches 0, it shatters and drops materials by “what it is made of × half” (see Durability and Breaking ). What drops pops out onto the ground; walk close and it flies into your bag. Things on the ground are picked up with E ; trees are chopped ( Woodcutting ), rocks are broken ( Mining ), crops are harvested ( Farming ). Smithing is the craft of turning ore into gear, in two steps: first smelt ore and coal into ingots beside a forge , then stand beside an anvil with a Smith Hammer and hammer the ingots into things. What you make is of the ingot's metal: an iron ingot makes an iron sword, a Steel Bar a steel sword; every thing has one anvil recipe for iron and one for steel (jewelry is iron and gold). The smithies of Firstlight Village , The Held Ground and Emberfall have a forge and anvil ready to use; once you learn Forge Builder you can build your own at home. Ore comes from Dawn Hill Mine north of Firstlight Village: reachable in Chapter 1, its iron veins and coal seams grow back one game day after being mined out; see Mining . x: Welcome to the OpenWorld Wiki OpenWorld is a 2D pixel role-playing game you play right in your web browser. The world's state and rules are code: the game itself is complete and can be played from start to finish; when you do something the world has never seen, the world learns it and remembers (see The World Learns ). You wake on Cloudtop with a little fairy, Lumi , at your side. The days grow shorter one by one, and the Long Night is returning. The Church of the Five Sufferings calls you onto the Pilgrim's Road, to seek out the five Seal-bearers .
